phonemes.desc: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — the 'sh' of English 'ship'. Classical Nahuatl writes this sound with the letter x.
Mid front [e]; the name ends on a short open vowel.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SHE-peh' — both vowels are short, the stress falls on the first syllable, and the x is never the English 'ks' or 'z' sound.

kin.label: Nahuatl
kin.form: xipehua, 'to flay, to peel (a fruit or a man)' — the verb at the root of the god's name (Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, s.v.)

kin.label: Nahuatl
kin.form: Tōtec, 'our lord' — the full cult name is Xipe Tōtec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One'

kin.label: Solar title
kin.form: Tlatlauhqui, 'the red one' — Xipe as 'Red Tezcatlipoca', lord of the west and patron of goldsmiths (Sahagún, Florentine Codex; Miller & Taube, s.v. Xipe Totec)

pronunciation.note: Xipe is Tier 2: the Classical Nahuatl x stands for [ʃ], but the ASCII string 'xipe' already encodes that phoneme, and the restoration 'Xipe' adds only capitalization — no distinctive letter that ASCII loses. The name means 'the flayed one', from xipehua.

domains.title: Xipe
domains.subtitle: Spring
domains.lead: Xipe — Xipe Tōtec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One' — is the Mexica god of spring, agriculture, and renewal whose priests wore the flayed skins of sacrificial captives for twenty days. Beneath the terror lay a farming theology: as the maize seed sheds its husk to sprout, so the god sheds his skin to feed the world. He was also patron of goldsmiths and lord of the west.

cards.name: The Flayed Lord
cards.desc: Xipe Tōtec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One': the deity who wears a second skin, honored from the shaft tombs of West Mexico to the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan.

cards.name: Spring
cards.desc: Patron of the planting season; his festival Tlacaxipehualiztli opened the agricultural year, when the maize sheds its husk (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2).

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: For twenty days his priests, dressed in flayed skins, walked from house to house — the renewal of the earth enacted in the streets.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form; the restoration returns the god's name to scholarly recognition.

symbols.name: Flayed human skin
symbols.meaning: His defining attribute — a second skin knotted at the wrists and ankles, the visible claim that the old covering must die for new life to emerge.

symbols.name: Maize husk
symbols.meaning: The theological key to his cult: the seed cannot germinate until it sheds its sheath, as the god shed his skin to feed humanity.

symbols.name: Temalacatl
symbols.meaning: The round gladiator stone on which captive warriors fought bound during Tlacaxipehualiztli before being sacrificed in his honor.

symbols.name: Pointed cap (copilli)
symbols.meaning: The conical headgear of his image, marking lordship and linking him to the solar-warrior complex of the western sky.

symbols.name: Chicahuaztli
symbols.meaning: The rattle staff he carries in codex imagery, an instrument of fertility whose sound accompanies the ancestral dances.

symbols.name: Knots at the back
symbols.meaning: In sculpture the god's own skin shows beneath the tied cords of the borrowed skin at his back — death worn as a garment.

mythology.lead: Xipe's mythology survives only in fragments: one late creation story, the great festival book of the Florentine Codex, and the uneasy testimony of Spanish friars. Pieced together, they reveal a god whose apparent cruelty is an agricultural theology — the flayed skin is the seed coat, and the death of the husk is the birth of the maize.

myths.title: The Lord Who Fed the World
myths.text: One late account, preserved in the colonial Histoyre du Mechique, tells that after the great flood the earth gave humanity nothing to eat, and the god Xipe Tōtec flayed himself so that people might be fed; for this reason his images are always shown wearing a human skin. Diego de Durán, who watched the rite's last performances in sixteenth-century Mexico, recorded the same conviction: the god had given his own covering for the world's sustenance. The friars were witnessing an agricultural allegory they only half understood. A maize seed cannot sprout until it splits and sheds its husk; the Mexica made that everyday miracle into a deity who wears the shed skin of a man. The myth teaches that feeding others is never costless: the renewal of the world is paid for with a skin.

myths.title: The Festival of the Flaying
myths.text: The Florentine Codex (Book 2) and Durán describe the great feast of the second veintena, roughly February–March: captives taken in war were dedicated at Yopico, the flayed lord's shrine in the Templo Mayor precinct; bound to the round temalacatl stone, they fought gladiatorial combats against seasoned warriors, then were stretched across the sacrificial stone. The priests then flayed the victims and wore their skins for twenty days, knotted at the wrists and ankles, visiting houses and receiving offerings as living images of the god, until the dried skins were laid away. Sahagún's informants named them tototectin, 'the flayed ones.' The rite horrified the friars and obsesses modern readers, but its logic was exact: at the start of the farming year the city reenacted the first flaying, so that what was done to the god might be done to the seed. Shed skin, shed husk, new season.

myths.title: The Red Lord of the West
myths.text: In the theological geography recorded from Sahagún's informants, Xipe Tōtec was also Tlatlauhqui, 'the red one' — the Red Tezcatlipoca, lord of the west, the quarter of the setting sun and of the earth's buried treasures. During Tlacaxipehualiztli the goldsmiths held their own feast, for Xipe was patron of their craft: gold, the Nahuatl-speakers called teocuitlatl, 'divine excrement', the sun's deposit in the earth's gut. The same festival that flayed a man to renew the fields also honored the men who pulled shining metal from the ground. Modern scholarship (Miller & Taube) has long noted the coherence: metal and maize are both riches that must be stripped out of a dead covering — ore from rock, grain from husk, flesh from skin. The red lord of the west governs them all.

myths.title: The God Made Flesh
myths.text: Central Mexicans did not think their gods watched the rite from afar. For the duration of the feast the chosen captive became an ixiptla — a 'representation', a living image of Xipe Tōtec — dressed, honored, and addressed as the god himself before he was killed and his skin assumed by the priests. Bernardino de Sahagún and Diego de Durán both describe how the impersonator was adorned and escorted through the city as though the deity had come down to walk among his people. The institution startled the friars into comparisons with the Christian God made man, and modern scholars such as Inga Clendinnen have made the ixiptla the key to understanding Mexica religion: a god who must enter a human body to renew the world, and leave it as a skin.

lore.syncretism: The Dominican Diego de Durán, watching Tlacaxipehualiztli in the decades after the Conquest, was struck that the feast fell near Holy Week — the god who wore a flayed skin commemorated at the season when Christians mourned a god who wore a body and lost it. The friars suppressed the rite, yet its imagery proved durable: in the Puebla and Guerrero regions, masked and costumed dance confraternities — ancestors of today's concheros and Danza Azteca — carried the flayed lord's memory in transformed dress. Twentieth-century revival movements such as the Mexicayotl circle reclaimed Xipe Tōtec as a figure of indigenous identity and renewal rather than barbarism. Comparative religion places him among the world's 'dying vegetation' gods, but the Mexica theology was stranger and more precise: not a god who dies like a plant, but a god who peels like a seed.
lore.culturalLegacy: Xipe Tōtec stands at the center of the modern debate over Aztec sacrifice — read by some as the theological heart of a sophisticated agricultural civilization, by others as evidence of state terror (Clendinnen, Townsend). His images anchor museum collections: the monolithic Xipe of the Templo Mayor Museum, wearing his knotted second skin, is among the most reproduced Aztec sculptures. Nahuatl lexicography (Karttunen, Lockhart) keeps his name etymologically alive, and Danza Azteca troupes across Mexico and the United States still perform in the spring season his festival once owned. For better and worse, the Flayed One is now the world's most recognizable emblem of Mexica religion.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Xipe Tōtec asks the question every farmer knows and every city forgets: what must die for something else to live? His answer is a skin. The maize seed does not negotiate with its husk; it splits it. The god does not sympathize with the covering; he wears it. In a culture that now separates death from dinner by an almost perfectly opaque supply chain, the Flayed One insists on the connection: your bread was once a seed's corpse, your gold was once a stone's wound.

To meditate on Xipe is to meditate on the cost of renewal. He is not a god of resurrection — nothing in the rite promises the flayed man his life back. He is a god of transfer: life moves, and something is always left behind. The friars saw only cruelty; the Mexica saw the farming year. Both were reading the same skin.
lore.archaeology: The earliest material witness to the flayed-skin complex comes from the shaft tombs of West Mexico (Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit, c. 200 BCE–500 CE), whose ceramic figures wear the flayed skins of other men — proof the imagery predates the Aztec state by centuries. At Tenochtitlan, the INAH excavations of the Templo Mayor precinct (from 1978) located Xipe's shrine, Yopico, and its caches; the Templo Mayor Museum preserves a monolithic Xipe Tōtec whose back shows the wearer's own skin beneath the knotted cords of the second skin. The cult's heartland lay among the Yope of the Guerrero coast and in the Puebla region, and the screenfold Codex Borgia (c. 1500) gives the god's fullest painted dossier.
